# The Peculiar Mathematics of Being Alive

I've been thinking lately about how we measure our lives in the smallest units imaginable, yet somehow these measurements never quite add up to anything coherent. We count our days, our hours, our accomplishments, as though the human experience were a ledger that could be balanced by the end of each month. But there's something fundamentally broken about this accounting system, and I think we all sense it, even if we don't talk about it much.

Consider the person who says they're "too busy" to call their mother. What does this mean, really? They have 168 hours in a week. Sleep takes roughly 56 of them. Work, say, 50 hours. Transportation, eating, hygiene, maybe another 30. That leaves 32 hours—more than a full day—yet somehow a 20-minute phone call is impossible. We're not actually measuring time; we're measuring attention. Or perhaps, to be more honest, we're measuring what we've unconsciously decided matters. The mathematics is perfectly logical, but the emotional mathematics tells a different story entirely.

This is the strange paradox of modern life: we've never had more control over our time, yet we've never felt more controlled by it. Our ancestors worked the fields because the work had to be done before winter. There was a natural endpoint to the day's labor. Now we can work forever—our emails follow us everywhere, our thoughts about work contaminate our leisure, and the thing we're working toward remains mysteriously, perpetually out of reach.

I wonder sometimes if this is why we've become so obsessed with productivity. It's an attempt to impose order on something fundamentally chaotic. If I just optimize my morning routine, if I batch my emails, if I use the Pomodoro Technique, maybe I'll actually feel like I've accomplished something. Maybe the hours will add up to a life. But hours don't add up to lives—moments do, and moments are irreducibly qualitative. You can't measure the depth of a conversation or the significance of a shared silence.

There's something about getting older that crystallizes this realization. When you're young, you have all the time in the world, so it doesn't matter—you waste it generously, extravagantly, without guilt. You're in a conversation at a party and you lose three hours without noticing. You read the same book twice just because you loved it. You don't know yet that time is finite, or rather, you know it intellectually but you don't *feel* it. There's a difference between knowing and feeling that seems to expand and contract depending on circumstances.

But somewhere along the way—and I think this happens at different ages for different people—you start to feel the shape of the ending. Not your ending specifically, maybe, but the ending. The fact that you'll never read every book, never visit every place, never master every skill you've always wanted to learn. You'll never have time for all of it. And this knowledge creates a kind of productive anxiety that we've turned into an entire industry. The self-improvement movement is essentially a denial of mortality dressed up as optimization.

What interests me is that some of the most memorable moments of our lives are the ones that are utterly "unproductive." A long walk with no destination. A conversation that circled back on itself five times. Sitting on a bench watching pigeons for no reason. Reading something just because it was beautiful, not because it would advance your career. These moments don't show up on any calendar or productivity tracker, yet they're often the ones we remember most vividly decades later.

I was speaking with someone recently who told me they hadn't taken a vacation in seven years. Not because they were forced to work the entire time, but because they felt guilty about stopping. That resonated with me because I recognized myself in it. There's a sort of Puritan logic that has burrowed deep into the American psyche—that worth is determined by what you produce, that rest is something you have to earn, that doing nothing is actually a kind of moral failure. We've turned existence itself into a hustle.

The tragic irony is that the things we need most—presence, connection, depth of understanding—can't be hurried. You can't optimize your way to meaningful friendship. You can't hack deeper love. You can't hack grief either, though God knows we try. We try to have our feelings efficiently, to process them quickly, to move through sadness or anger in discrete, manageable chunks.

But grief, real grief, doesn't respect project timelines. It takes the time it takes.

I think this is why we're all so tired. We're not tired because we're working too hard, exactly. We're tired because we're holding two contradictory beliefs simultaneously: that time is infinitely precious and therefore we can't waste a single moment of it, AND that we can somehow get control over time through sheer force of will. Both things might be true, but living in the tension between them is exhausting.

The alternative would require something like faith, or at least acceptance. It would mean believing that a day spent reading in bed matters just as much as a day spent being productive. It would mean trusting that an unmeasured life can still be a good life. It would mean accepting that you'll never do it all, read it all, be it all—and somehow being okay with that.

I'm not sure I've achieved that. I'm writing this essay partly as a way to procrastinate on other things I'm supposed to be doing, which seems pretty on-brand for the human condition. But maybe the point isn't to achieve perfect peace with the meaninglessness of our time measurements. Maybe the point is to notice when we're doing it, to catch ourselves trying to optimize our way out of being human, and to sometimes—not always, but sometimes—choose the unmeasured moment anyway.

The irony is that this essay took me about an hour to write, which I'll report to myself as "productive time," even though I'm not sure it actually changed anything about how I live. Maybe that's okay. Maybe that's just how it works.
